meaning:
21 is referencing his record deal with Epic Records. An advance is a sum of money given by the label to the artist for them to live off while producing an album, which then has to be paid back from sales of that album before any royalties can be claimed. 21 is looking at his advance wondering if he’ll manage to pay it back and actually profit from his releases.

However, he then praises his label for allowing him to own his masters, which are very valuable as it gives an artist the legal right to make money out of their recordings through collecting royalties and sync licensing their recorded music to film, TV, adverts etc. Many artists are fighting to obtain ownership of their masters such as Kanye West, Taylor Swift, who’s re-recording her albums to own their masters, and Jay-Z, who’s masters are reportedly worth up to $50 million. line: My dog lost his life and it changed me (Damn) I’m poppin’ Percocets ’cause the pain deep
vault_lines: My dog lost his life and it changed me (Damn)
meaning:
On 21 Savage’s 21st birthday, he and his best friend Johnny were doing a deal which quickly turned sour, and they were shot at by two assailants. Johnny was subsequently shot in the head and killed. While 21 attempted to return fire, he was still shot six times. When asked if he thought he was going to die, 21 responded:

Yeah, [there was a] whole lot of blood loss. A whole lot of blood loss. But I guess they say your adrenaline be rushing. So you don’t really feel it, when it’s going on.

While 21 also lost his brother Tayman in a botched drug deal and another one of his friends – Larry – was also gunned down the following reference to Percocets makes it likely that he is referring to the incident on his 21st.

According to an interview he gave on The Breakfast Club in 2016, the incident introduced him to the painkiller Percocet, as he was given a prescription in the hospital to help him cope with the bullet wounds. In his own words:

I had about five surgeries, I got addicted to ‘em and I couldn’t get off of 'em. Know what I’m sayin’? That’s the hospital’s fault, really. Know what I’m sayin'? And then I look up and now it’s a fashion to do Percs when I was poppin' ‘em was nobody poppin’ no Percs. People was but it wasn’t like how it is now, know what I’m sayin'?

Safe to say most would need some kind of pain relief after living through what 21 has been through.

The Intratec TEC-9, commonly abbreviated to TEC, was a semi-automatic pistol that sold over 250,000 units during its tenure.



The TEC was first introduced in 1985 and was made by the firearm manufacturer, Intratec. It gained a negative reputation in the 1990s for its association with street gangs and shootings. It was infamously used in July 1993’s 101 California Street shooting and April 1999’s Columbine High School massacre.

Following the above controversies, the production of the gun was discontinued in 2001. Although the gun is federally legal  and accessible in several used gun markets, it is banned in several U.S. states.

21 Savage plays on the abbreviation TEC to allude to technical fouls, an extreme penalty in basketball. 21 compares getting technical fouls in basketball to shooting his enemies.

Although 21 raps about using the TEC in this song, he mocked its usage on Metro Boomin’s November 2018 track, “10 Freaky Girls”:

You a rookie (You a rookie), I’m a vet (I’m a vet)
That’s why I got a Glock, you got a TEC (Got a TEC)

line: Why you got a twelve-car garage?
vault_lines: Why you got a twelve-car garage?
meaning:
This rhetorical question occurs multiple times throughout 21 Savage’s works; a year after releasing “No Heart”, he is featured on Post Malone’s song Rockstar saying,

Savage, why you got a twelve car garage/ And you only got six cars?"

While 21 doesn’t elaborate much in “No Heart” regarding his reasoning for having such a large place to store his cars, he clarifies in “Rockstar” that the size of his garage is notably peculiar given that he only owns enough cars to fill half of his enormous garage.

On the surface level, this is a pretty simple line: 21 Savage is conveying the idea that he uses his excessive amounts of money to purchase unnecessarily large luxury items that he doesn’t need, simply for the purpose of flexing on others. However, there might be a deeper implication here.

When he clarifies in “Rockstar” that he only has 6 cars, Savage could be telling his audience that he isn’t able to match his luxurious lifestyle in every area of his character; he has a huge garage, but not enough cars to fill such a garage. This might work as a metaphor for the idea that 21 wants to convey: his outwardly luxurious lifestyle (represented by the 12 car garage) is unable to be filled by what is within (represented by his ownership of only 6 cars).

In this sequence, 21 Savage humorously codifies a woman’s sexual history into a mock hierarchy of worthiness, blending sexual bravado with satirical commentary. On the surface, he’s establishing arbitrary thresholds: ten or fewer partners earns respect (“queen”), fewer than nine implies casual intimacy without protection, and fewer than eight elevates her to marriageable status. The rapid shifts in these criteria exaggerate how absurd and contradictory the fixation on sexual pasts can be, turning a common trope in hip-hop into a deliberately over-the-top joke.

This passage also reveals something deeper about 21 Savage’s commentary on masculinity and sexual politics in rap. He’s simultaneously flaunting dominance and control—deciding who’s “worthy” and who’s not—while satirizing the often hypocritical and performative ways men measure women’s value. The specificity of the numbers (“ten,” “nine,” “eight”) gives the bar a pseudo-scientific absurdity, as if he’s presenting a serious formula, which contrasts hilariously with the ridiculousness of the content.

Additionally, the lines reflect the album’s broader tone in POP IT and What Happened to the Streets?—a mix of excessive flexing, humor, and social commentary. By openly quantifying sexual experience, 21 Savage highlights the inherent absurdity of these standards while still flexing sexual dominance, showing how trap music often blends threat, desire, and satire into a single punchline. The humor, exaggeration, and bravado all work together to make this bar memorable, shocking, and culturally resonant, capturing both the playfulness and the critique embedded in modern trap lyricism.

This bar also connects to the way Latto is always talking about her low body count, that’s where this wordplay comes from. He’s actually complimenting her. 21 frequently hyperbolizes experiences of wealth, sex, and violence, using extreme imagery to assert power while signaling self-awareness about the performative nature of these claims. The result is a line that functions on multiple levels: a sexual flex, a satirical jab at cultural obsessions with women’s pasts, and a testament to 21 Savage’s ability to combine humor with menace seamlessly.

In this opening passage, 21 Savage delivers what many scholars consider the definitive modern meditation on affirmation. While casual listeners may mistake these repeated “yeahs” as simple ad-libs, closer analysis reveals a masterclass in minimalistic expression.

By saying yeah four times — and then daring to say yeah again — 21 challenges the boundaries of language itself. Each “yeah” is identical in spelling, pronunciation, and meaning, a poetic symmetry so precise that it borders on mathematical perfection. Some critics argue this sequence rivals the structural economy of Hemingway; others place it closer to postmodern existentialism, where meaning is found in repetition, not variation.

The subtle shift from “yeah” to “ye-yeah” represents what many interpret as Savage’s commentary on the instability of identity in late-stage capitalism — a linguistic flourish so daring that few contemporary writers would attempt it.

line: I done been through all the trials and tribulations, now I’m smilin’ (21)
vault_lines: I done been through all the trials and tribulations, now I'm smilin' (21)
meaning:
At face value, this line appears to be a simple braggadocious bar in which 21 Savage laments on how far he has come in his career since selling drugs to get by on the harsh streets of Atlanta, Georgia; however, upon analysis, it appears that 21 may very well be referencing the overarching theme of the Saw franchise.

In the films, John Kramer, the Jigsaw killer, never intended to kill his victims; rather, his intention was to put them through a series of deadly scenarios, referred to as “games” or “tests”, in which they were forced to inflict pain upon themselves, or others, in order to escape. These tests were typically symbolic of what Jigsaw perceived as a flaw in each victim’s moral character or life and were intended to instil in his victims a new appreciation for life, with some of his victims, most notably Amanda Young and Lawrence Gordon, joining him in his mission.

In this line, 21 compares the hardships he endured throughout his life to those experienced by Jigsaws' victims, ultimately reaching the same enlightened outcome as (most of) those who survive.

To be ten steps ahead means to be more prepared, skilled, or successful than your adversaries; able to outmaneuver or outpace someone or something.

In this line, 21 laments on the savvy and prowess he obtained by selling drugs in the cruel conditions of Atlanta, Georgia, which he was subsequently able to use in the music industry to garner immense commercial success and critical claim.

21 compares his skills to that of John Kramer, also known as Jigsaw, the primary antagonist of the Saw franchise.

Throughout the series, Kramer always stayed ten steps ahead of his victims and the police, allowing him to unknowingly capture his victims and place them in elaborate traps, testing their will to survive.

Alternatively, 21 may be comparing the way he sneaks up on and tortures his opps to that of Kramer, who donned a pig mask throughout the series to capture his victims.

“Penitentiary chances” are high-risk, illegal acts that could lead to jail time or imprisonment. 21 Savage says he is willing to take these risks for any dollar amount.

Taking “penitentiary chances” is a common trope in hip-hop, but the phrase finds one of its earliest uses on a medium in a 1907 issue of McClure’s Magazine, where it discusses professional criminals in Chicago who were willing to risk going to jail in order to help politicians get votes in certain wards.

After 1907, the phrase is seen again in Sterling B. Scott’s 1994 novel The Weeds of Society. The narrator at one point says:

No longer would I be a small-time street hustler taking penitentiary chances for nickels and dimes.

The last piece of media that seems to use this outside of rap is a 1998 low-budget indie film directed by Quiroz brothers, Jose and Eduardo, called Penitentiary Chances. The film is a prequel to Veteranos and is credited with being the beginning of the urban movie genre. It can be viewed in its entirety on YouTube.
